reference.source: Primer on the Metabolic Bone Diseases / Williams Textbook of Endocrinology
clinicalPearls: Caused by activating mutations in the FGF23 gene that protect the hormone from cleavage, prolonging its phosphaturic action
Inheritance is autosomal dominant but penetrance and age of onset are variable, so some carriers present in childhood and others only in adolescence or adulthood
Biochemistry mirrors other FGF23-driven states: hypophosphataemia with renal phosphate wasting and inappropriately low or normal 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D
A characteristic feature is fluctuating severity, with disease activity influenced by iron status, since iron deficiency drives increased FGF23 production
Childhood presentation resembles rickets with bowing, growth impairment, and dental abscesses, whereas adult presentation resembles osteomalacia with bone pain and weakness
Some individuals experience spontaneous improvement or waxing and waning of symptoms, unlike the persistent course of X-linked disease
Management uses oral phosphate salts with active vitamin D (calcitriol), and correcting coexisting iron deficiency may reduce FGF23-mediated phosphate wasting
reference.pathophysiology: ADHR results from missense mutations at the FGF23 cleavage site that render the intact hormone resistant to proteolytic inactivation. Stabilised FGF23 accumulates and suppresses renal sodium-phosphate cotransport, producing phosphaturia and hypophosphataemia, while also inhibiting 1-alpha-hydroxylase so that 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is inappropriately low or normal. Because iron deficiency stimulates FGF23 transcription while normally increasing cleavage, in ADHR the uncleavable mutant accumulates during iron-deficient states, explaining the disease's characteristic fluctuation and its links to menstruation, pregnancy, and growth. The net result is defective mineralisation manifesting as rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.
additionalInvestigations: Serum phosphate with tubular reabsorption of phosphate indices to demonstrate renal wasting
Calcium, parathyroid hormone, alkaline phosphatase, and vitamin D metabolites including 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D
Intact FGF23 measurement, typically elevated or inappropriately normal
Iron studies, since iron deficiency can precipitate or worsen phosphate wasting
Radiographs of the wrists, knees, and long bones for rachitic or osteomalacic change
FGF23 gene sequencing to confirm an activating cleavage-site mutation
redFlags: Progressive limb deformity or growth failure in an affected child
New or worsening symptoms coinciding with iron-deficient states such as pregnancy or heavy menstruation
Recurrent dental abscesses indicating poorly controlled disease
Development of nephrocalcinosis or hyperparathyroidism during treatment
reference.prognosis: Course is variable, ranging from spontaneous resolution to persistent phosphate wasting; with phosphate and active vitamin D therapy and attention to iron status, most affected children achieve improved growth and bone health, though monitoring for treatment complications is required.
pitfalls: Assuming a uniform course and missing episodic flares tied to iron deficiency
Failing to check and correct iron status, which modulates FGF23-driven phosphate wasting
Confusing ADHR with the more persistent X-linked form and mislabelling family inheritance
Overtreating with active vitamin D and phosphate, risking nephrocalcinosis and secondary hyperparathyroidism
references: Primer on the Metabolic Bone Diseases and Disorders of Mineral Metabolism
